paras: The Homestead drug store siege was a threatened lynching at Homestead, Pennsylvania, on the evening of July 16, 1882, when a crowd surrounded a drug store where a man named Fowley had taken refuge after shooting a man named Critchlow. The crowd demanded Fowley and threatened to break in, but it dispersed without violence and he was jailed in Pittsburgh the next morning. Later reports tied the quarrel to a strike at the Bessemer Steel Company's mill, and none of the reports gives the race of anyone involved.

In the summer of 1882 the blooming department of the Bessemer Steel Company at Homestead was on strike, and Fowley was described as 'a non-Union man' who worked at the mill. Critchlow, the man he shot, was called 'the striker' in a Pittsburgh dispatch.

According to a Homestead special carried by the wire, Fowley was milking a cow on the evening of July 16 when a number of 'half drunken men' attacked him. He drew a revolver and, in what the report called self defense, shot Critchlow in the stomach, a wound the first dispatch described as fatal. A September account described the same clash as Critchlow attacking Fowley 'during an incipient riot'.

Fowley escaped to a drug store, and a large crowd of Critchlow's friends followed and demanded that he be turned over to them, for the purpose, 'it is thought, of lynching'. The crowd threatened to batter down the doors and take him out by force. A dispatch the next day said the mob stayed around the store until late at night but did not try to carry out its threats.

On the morning of July 17 Fowley, printed as 'Fowler', was brought to Pittsburgh and lodged in jail, while a crowd followed him to the station throwing a few stones. The same report said Critchlow was 'not dangerously hurt'. No report of a charge, trial or court outcome for the shooting was found.

The matter returned when the strike ended in September 1882, as union men in the blooming department refused to work because Manager Williams had discharged Critchlow. Fowley, who had kept working at the mill, resigned 'in order to save trouble', and a later telegram said both men had been relieved from duty and work would resume.

The first wire item ran on July 17 in the St. Paul Daily Globe under the headline 'In Danger of Lynching', and in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer as 'A Tragedy at Homestead'. The Washington National Republican printed it in a column of briefs, and two of the printings carried a July 10 dateline although they described events of 'this evening'. The wire took Fowley's side, calling his attackers 'half drunken' and his shot self defense, and the Globe's follow-up called the affair 'The Rumpus at Homestead'.

By September the case appeared only as a detail in reports on the settlement of the iron workers' strike, framed as a test of the Amalgamated Association's rules. None of the papers mentioned the race of Fowley, Critchlow or the crowd.

The first dispatch said Critchlow was fatally shot, but the Pittsburgh follow-up a day later said he was not dangerously hurt, and the September reports show him alive and employed at the mill until his discharge.

accounts.label: Wire report (Homestead special)
accounts.gist: Fowley, milking a cow, was attacked by half-drunken men and fired in self defense, 'fatally' wounding Chritchlow; Critchlow's friends then besieged him in a drug store.

accounts.label: Pittsburgh follow-up
accounts.gist: The mob dispersed without violence, Fowler was jailed in Pittsburgh, and Cutchlow, 'the striker', was not dangerously hurt.

accounts.label: September labor report
accounts.gist: Critchlow attacked Fowley, a non-Union man, during an 'incipient riot' at the strike-bound mill; Fowley shot him and kept working until the settlement.

framing.detail: Brief wire item headed 'In Danger of Lynching' or 'A Tragedy at Homestead', accepting Fowley's self-defense account and calling the attackers 'half drunken'.
The follow-up, 'The Rumpus at Homestead', and the September items treat the case as a strike incident, not a racial one.

conflicts.note: All three ran on July 17 and say 'this evening'; the July 10 dateline is likely a misprint, and the July 18 follow-up dated July 17 refers to 'last night'.
The later report is better evidence; Critchlow was discharged from the mill in September (A7).
